examples: This is a program for children.
I explained the terms simply for beginners.
This product is for businesses.
We will change it to the specifications for overseas markets.
We placed an ad in a women's magazine.
This factory mainly builds cars for the American market.
fields.explain:
Used often in marketing, instruction manuals, and user segmentation.
Neutral/formal; can stand alone as a modifier:学生向け割引.
The target can be broad (海外向け) or narrow (上級者向け).

• Indicates that something is “aimed at” or “designed for” a specific group/target.
• Carries the nuance of the intention of the maker/creator: “directing a product/content toward …”.
• Different from ～向き (suitable): ～向け means “oriented toward, intended specifically for”; ～向き means “suitable in general”.
fields.notes:
1) ～向け and ～向き are easily confused.
→ ～向け means “for/aimed at a target”, usually products, information, or services directed at N.
2) There are 2 usages in the data (ghichu=1 and ghichu=2).
→ The meaning “for” differs from “working toward a goal” (～に向けて).
3) Look at what comes after this phrase.
→ If it is “a product/material for someone”: ～向け.
→ If it is “an action toward a goal”: ～に向けて.
explain: ◎ A way of saying what kind of person something is suitable for.
examples: 1. これは女性向けの雑誌です。
This is a magazine for women.
2. このホテルは、旅行者向けのサイトで見つけました。
I found this hotel on a website for travelers.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～向き: both 子供向き and 子供向け are possible, but 向け emphasizes “aimed at/designed for”.
Confusing it with ～行き: X 東京向けの電車 → it should be 東京行きの電車.
Using 向け for an immediate personal action: X 私向けに席を取って → sounds odd; better: 私のために席を取って.

fields.meaning: In the middle of, right while
examples: The phone rang in the middle of the meeting.
The power went out while I was taking the exam.
Please don't leave your seat in the middle of the meal.
In the middle of the presentation, I couldn't find the materials.
It started raining in the middle of the construction work.
fields.explain:
Used in both spoken and written language; slightly more formal than ～間に.
The first clause sets a point in time when something is “in progress”; the second clause is usually an interrupting event.
Unnatural with stative verbs such as知っている・分かっている; actions/activities are preferred.
Often used with activity nouns:会議・授業・試合・手術・面接・作業.

• “Right while… was going on, … (usually an interruption/something unwanted)”
• Emphasizes the peak moment of an action/activity, stronger than ～間に.
• Usually used with short/limited actions (会議・試験・食事), rarely with static, lasting states.
• The second clause is often a mishap, an obstacle, or an unexpected announcement; but it can also be a neutral event.
fields.notes:
• The form “最中だ/です” is often used to set the scene: 会議の最中です。
• In polite language: ～最中にございます is rarely used, so keep ～最中に/～最中です.
• To emphasize what should not be done: ～最中に…しないでください／～最中はご遠慮ください。
meaning_vi: While doing that, right at that moment... (Expresses that something unexpected happens.)
examples: 1. ①　シャワーを浴びている最中に
While I was taking a shower...
2. ②　シャワーを浴びている最中に、客が来た。
A guest came while I was taking a shower.
3. ③　引っ越しの最中に雨が降り出した。
It started raining while we were moving. | Sentence-final form: ～最中だ
mistakes: Forgetting “の” with nouns: incorrect “会議最中に” → correct “会議の最中に”.
Using the dictionary form of V: incorrect “食事する最中に” → correct “食事している最中に”.
Applying it to a static state (知っている最中に) is unnatural.
Confusing it with ～間に: exam questions often test the nuance “right at the moment” vs “during the period”.

rows: Midpoint, peak; strong sense of interruption
<ruby>試験<rt>しけん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>最中<rt>さいちゅう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>
Does not focus on the exact midpoint
<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みの<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>
Just as about to/in the middle of/just after
Fine-tunes the point in time; neutral nuance
<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけるところに<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>
Focus on the process, not necessarily the peak
<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>る<ruby>途中<rt>とちゅう</rt></ruby>で<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>

examples: Lately work has been a bit busy, and I'm short on sleep.
Because of the rain, the start of the game is running a little late.
He always seems a bit nervous during meetings.
I think I'm coming down with a cold, so I'll go home early today.
I've been eating too much, and I've started to put on a little weight.
I'm feeling a bit tired.
fields.explain:
Formation: N/ Vます-stem directly +気味; does not attach to i-adjectives or な-adjectives.
Degree: “a little/rather”, not heavy; for a strong degree use ～気がする, ～っぽい, ～過ぎ, ～ぎみでもない.
Context: neutral to polite; can be used at work when describing a situation.
Often used with words that have a somewhat negative tone:疲れ,太り,不足,下降,遅れ; positive ones are less common (上向き気味exists but is rare).

• “A bit, a feeling of”: expresses a mild degree, not yet clear but tending to appear.
• Range of meaning: often used for physical condition (疲れ気味, 太り気味), mental state (緊張気味, 焦り気味), situations (遅れ気味, 下降気味).
• Highly objective: spoken as an observation of oneself/others without strong judgment.
• Different from っぽい: 気味 emphasizes “a slight current tendency”, っぽい emphasizes “resembling/leaning toward a quality, sometimes subjective, colloquial”.
fields.notes:
• Written forms: 忙し気味／忙しぎみ are both seen; the hiragana form ぎみ is common in learning materials.
• With fixed Sino-Japanese words: 目つきが悪い vs 目つき気味(rare) → prefer familiar state nouns.
• In spoken language, it can be used with adverbs for slight exaggeration: ちょっと疲れ気味, 少し太り気味. meaning_vi: Seems, a bit, a feeling that ⏐ explain: Expresses the meaning “to be in such a state, to have such a tendency”. Often used for things with a bad meaning. ⏐ examples: 1. 残業続きで、疲れ気味だ。
I've been working overtime nonstop, so I'm a bit tired.
2. 新入社員は緊張気味の顔をしていた。
The new employee looked a bit nervous.
mistakes: Wrong word class: × 寒い気味 → Correct: 寒気味 is unnatural; use 寒気がする／寒がりだ.
Wrong degree: 気味 only means “a bit”; to say strongly “very tired”, use すごく疲れている, 疲れすぎだ, ぐったりだ.
Confusing it with ～がち: 遅れ気味 (a bit late) ≠ 遅れがち (often late).
JLPT: trick questions ask you to choose between 気味/っぽい/がち based on the nuance “slight – frequent – resembling”.

rows: Colloquial, subjective, wide range of combinations
<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>っぽい／ミスしがちっぽい(×)
Stronger than <ruby>気味<rt>きみ</rt></ruby>, with a negative nuance
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れがち／<ruby>病気<rt>びょうき</rt></ruby>がち
Emphasizes a subjective feeling, full clause
<ruby>疲<rt>つか</rt></ruby>れている<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>がする

fields.meaning: To be scheduled, to be decided ～
examples: The graduation ceremony is scheduled to be held here tomorrow.
The rule is that 60 points or more is a pass.
A meeting about the new project is scheduled to be held tomorrow.
It has been decided that I will be transferred to Osaka.
fields.explain: Used to emphasize that the matter was not decided by the subject themselves but was determined, set, or ordered by other people or other factors

examples: The moment I opened the window, a strong wind blew in.
As soon as I drank the alcohol, my face turned red.
fields.explain:
Used when something happens right when an action has just been done.
The second clause does not use sentence patterns with an active meaning (transitive verbs), the causative form, or obligation

examples: When registering, please present your ID.
When you visit our office, please give your name at the reception desk.
This document is required when entering Japan.
When using it, please be sure to change your password.
In the event of a disaster, please refrain from using the elevators.
fields.explain:
“際（に）” takes “は/には” to mark the topic: ～際には (more emphatic than ～際に).
Usually placed in the first clause; the second clause is an instruction, rule, or polite request.
Common nouns: ご利用／ご来場／ご来店／ご乗車／入学／登録／申請／購入／訪問。
Not used for very everyday, momentary feelings; use とき in casual situations.

• Expresses the point in time when an action/event occurs, equivalent to “when/at the time”, but formal; used a lot in instructions, signs, and company emails.
• Often used with expressions of request, caution, or prohibition: ご注意ください／ご連絡ください／持参してください／ご遠慮ください。
• Not used for daily habits or casual conversation; use とき instead.
fields.notes:
• “際” is read さい; do not confuse it with きわ (meaning “edge”). In this grammar point it is read only さい.
• “際は/際には” often appear on forms/signs; adding には makes it more emphatic and formal.
• Common 敬語 pairs: ごV-ます＋の際（に）／V-辞＋際（に）＋お/ご～ください。
• Variant: ～際（に）は
mistakes: Using it in casual conversation sounds stiff: × 映画を見る際にポップコーン買う？ → とき is more natural.
Forgetting “には” when emphasis is needed: ご利用の際には is better than ご利用の際 when you want to be polite/emphatic.
Confusing it with 場合: for “in case of trouble”, use 場合, not 際.
JLPT: ～折に (very polite) and ～際に are easily confused; pay attention to the context of letters/cards.

fields.meaning:
～の可能性もある
There is also a possibility that…, it's not that one can't…
examples: It's not that I don't eat it, but I don't like it very much.
Quitting drinking and smoking is hard, but it's not impossible.
It's not that I don't eat chicken, but I don't like it very much.
"If we run, we can still make it. Let's hurry!"
fields.explain: Used when you want to say that you are not denying the matter or thing itself, but want to express a reason/ a lower degree compared with a negative

examples: It doesn't hurt at all, so don't worry.
His explanation isn't difficult at all.
This movie wasn't interesting at all.
Even though he's tired, he won't rest at all.
She doesn't seem to suspect me at all.
fields.explain:
Place 少しも/すこしも before the negated word to emphasize “not even a little”.
Suitable for both written and spoken language; ちっとも〜ない leans toward spoken language and casual speech.
Can be used with the past, potential, and volition:少しもできなかった／少しも行く気がしない.

• “Not … at all/not … one bit”. Emphasizes a degree of zero.
• Used to completely negate a feeling/state/action.
• Compared with 全然〜ない/まったく〜ない: milder than まったく, equal to or milder than 全然 depending on the context.
• Spelling: both 少しも and すこしも are correct; 少しも is common in written language.
fields.notes:
• An emphatic word can be inserted between: 少しも全く覚えていない（written language, double emphasis）.
• In polite communication, avoid overusing it toward the listener so as not to sound extreme.
• Rhetorical interrogative form: 少しも悪くない？（Not bad at all, right?）
mistakes: Using it with an affirmative: 少しも must be followed by a negative. 誤）少しも大丈夫 → 正）少しも大丈夫ではない。
Wrong degree: まったく＞全然≧少しも＞ちっとも（relative; depends on the context).
Spelling mistake: すくしも× → すこしも／少しも〇.
Wrong position: it must come before the negated element to have full effect.

rows: Casual, sometimes with a complaining nuance
ちっとも<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>くならない
Strong, common; in modern usage can be used with the affirmative (colloquial)
<ruby>全然<rt>ぜんぜん</rt></ruby><ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からない

examples: The weather is bad. So I'm not going out today.
I'm new, so there's still a lot I don't know.
The exam is tomorrow, so please go to bed early.
This is a danger zone. Therefore, please do not enter.
He's the person in charge, so you should talk to him directly.
Demand is increasing. Therefore, we will increase production.
fields.explain:
Used when presenting logic, in presentations, and in business emails: “A (information). ですから、B (conclusion/recommendation)”.
In conversation, ですから can begin a response: “ ですから、先ほど申し上げたとおり…”.
Compared with だから: more polite, less direct; suits formal settings.
Not used to express strong emotion; when you need to emphasize firm reasoning, use したがって.
Within a sentence, “Aですから、B” is usually used when A is a noun/na-adj; with verbs/い-adj use ～から/～ので: 「雨が降る から、…」.

• Main meaning: States a conclusion/result based on the information/condition just mentioned: “therefore/so/thus”.
• Politeness: More polite than だから; often used in presentations, news, and refined written language.
• Position: Usually at the start of the result clause, separate from the reason clause (the previous sentence).
• Two usages to distinguish:

Independent conjunction: 「A。ですから、B。」
Linking within a sentence: 「Aですから、B。」 (A is a noun/na-adj + です)

• Independent conjunction: 「A。ですから、B。」
• Linking within a sentence: 「Aですから、B。」 (A is a noun/na-adj + です)
• Nuance: Objective, polite reasoning; avoids strong/overly personal emotion.
fields.notes:
• To soften a request: 「危険ですから、こちらへお願いします。」 sounds more polite than 「危ないから…」.
• In a debate, starting a sentence with ですから to lead to the conclusion makes it coherent and avoids an abrupt “change of direction”.
• Instead of repeating ですから in a row, alternate with それで/したがって to make the text natural. explain: Used for a sentence that is the result or consequence of the previous sentence. The preceding sentence usually states a reason, a judgment, or a natural result ⏐ examples: 1. 「天気予報では午後から雨だそうです。ですから、傘を持っていったほうがいいですよ。」
According to the weather forecast, it will rain from the afternoon. So you should take an umbrella.
2. 明日から旅行に行きます。ですから、申し訳ありませんが、来週のパーテイーには出席できません。
I'm going on a trip from tomorrow. So, I'm sorry, but I can't attend the party next week
mistakes: Using ですから in a casual context among friends → sounds distant; use だから/それで instead.
Confusing “Aです。ですから、B。” with “Aだから、B。” When A is a noun/na-adj, both are possible, but the nuance differs.
Using ですから to state a strongly subjective reason (anger) → not appropriate; use だって/だもん, which carry emotion.
JLPT: a trap distinguishing それで vs ですから (both translated as “so”): それで leans toward a sequence of events; ですから emphasizes a logical conclusion.

rows: Polite; used as a conjunction or as “Aですから、B”.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>です。ですから、<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>です。
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れる。だから<ruby>先<rt>さき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>って。
Continuative link; more about connected events than logical reason.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だった。それで、<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>にいた。
<ruby>需要<rt>じゅよう</rt></ruby><ruby>増<rt>ぞう</rt></ruby>。したがって、<ruby>価格<rt>かかく</rt></ruby><ruby>上昇<rt>じょうしょう</rt></ruby>。
Links within a sentence to state a direct reason.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>なので<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>します。

examples: No matter how tired I am, I keep my promises.
No matter how much I practice, I just don't improve.
No matter how busy you are, time with your family is important.

fields.explain:
For emphasis, いくら／どれほど can be used instead of どんなに (similar nuance).
The second clause is usually a clause stating a firm position/volition or a general judgment.
Suitable for both spoken and written language; carries the nuance of “regardless of any degree”.

• Extreme concession: “no matter to what degree… (the result/view does not change)”.
• Emphasis with どんなに: covers every degree, every way.
• The second clause usually expresses an unchanging result/volition/evaluation, or has a nuance of being constant and hard to change.
fields.notes:
• It can be repeated: どんなにどんなに… but repetition is usually avoided so it doesn't sound heavy.
• A negative second clause is not required; both affirmative and negative are common depending on the content.
• Combine with potential verbs to emphasize “regardless of effort”: どんなに頑張ってもできない。
mistakes: Confusing it with ～ことか: one is a condition, the other an exclamation.
Wrong form: Aい→Aくても; Aな→Aでも; N→Nでも; V→Vてでも? (a different pattern, do not confuse).
Dropping も: “ても/でも” is required; without “も” the structure is incorrect.

fields.meaning: Spoken-language form of the structure 「なければならない／なくてはいけない」
fields.connection: Vなければならない → Vなきゃ・Vなく(っ)ちゃ / Vないと（spoken language）
examples: I have to buy it.

fields.explain:
まったく usually comes before the negative part to emphasize the idea “not even a little”.
Can be used at many language levels, from casual speech to written language.
If it is not used with ～ない but with a positive adjective (まったく素晴らしい), the meaning changes to “really…”, “truly…”.
In conversation, when used alone, “まったく！” → expresses a complaint: “I can't stand it!”, “Honestly!”.

•
まったく～ない is used to emphasize a degree of absolute negation: “not … at all”, “never …”, “not even a little …”.

• Usually used with negative verbs, adjectives, or nouns: ～ない・～くない・～ではない.
• Has a strong nuance, sometimes expressing surprise, complaint, or disappointment.
fields.notes:
• In written language, the kanji 全く can be used instead of まったく.
• With the positive meaning (まったく～だ), you need to distinguish it clearly when translating to avoid misunderstanding.
• Example: まったく君は… → “Honestly, you… (slightly reproachful)”. explain: Used to assert that something does not exist at all or cannot happen at all. ⏐ examples: 1. 私はまったく泳げない。
I can't swim at all
2. 彼が怒っている理由は、私にはまったくわからない。
I have no idea at all why he is angry
3. 前とは違うまったく新しい計画を立てた。
We made a completely new plan, different from before
mistakes: Confusing it with ぜんぜん → まったく feels stronger, not even a little.
Using まったく with a non-negative word → the meaning changes to “really…” and is no longer negative.
The JLPT often tests the nuance: まったく～ない vs 全然～ない.
